items.title: Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England in the 1680s
items.claim: Why did French Huguenots come to England?

options.text: They were invited as agricultural labour by William III
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1598) in 1685, removing Protestant rights — around 50,000 fled to England, with major settlements in Spitalfields, Soho and Canterbury
They were exiled by James II for Jacobite sympathies
Famine in Brittany drove migration in the 1680s

items.reveal:
The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (October 1685) made Protestant worship illegal in France. Perhaps 200,000-400,000 Huguenots fled total — to England, the Dutch Republic, Brandenburg, the Cape and the American colonies.

In England they brought silk-weaving (Spitalfields), gunmaking, watchmaking, banking (the Courtauld and Bosanquet families). 'Refugee' as an English word enters the language from the Huguenot experience.

Charles II had already extended denizenship to French Protestants in 1681. Anti-Catholic sentiment made absorption relatively smooth.
items.why: Migration history in Britain is much older than the 20th century. The Huguenot case is the classic example of refugees whose skills shaped an industrial sector — and whose absorption was made easier by religious alignment.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.
